title: Microbiome Assessment In Infants At Risk For Hypoxic Ischemic Encephalopathy
summary: The entirety of the naturally colonizing organisms in the intestine (the so-called "intestinal microbiome") is an important link between the intestine and the brain (the so-called gut-brain axis) and influences the development of both organ systems through various metabolic processes. Especially in the first months of newborns' lives, the microbiome develops very dynamically, but is also susceptible to disruptive factors. A significantly more difficult postnatal adaptation of a newborn (a so-called oxygen deficiency during birth - "perinatal asphyxia") could lead to certain changes in the microbiome or in the profile of the metabolites of the affected child. In these cases, cooling therapy (a so-called hypothermia treatment) is usually used, which could have a significant influence on the microbiome composition. The MARIE study examines the composition of the microbiome and metabolic profile in infants with severe adjustment disorder before, during and after cooling therapy and compares it with healthy newborns. Furthermore, the study follows the children and their families over a period of 5 years and observes the long-term health development of the study participants and analyzes the composition of the intestinal microbiome and corresponding metabolic profiles.

interventions.name: Multicenter, prospective observational study of newborns with perinatal asphyxia under standardized intensive care (clinical data collection) and neurological diagnostics (EEG/aEEG, GMA) including imaging (MRI) followed by longitudinal examination of the health development and specifics of the micro

Mature newborns from existing birth cohorts or healthy newborns at the corresponding study centers or, if applicable, siblings of the affected child household controls act as a healthy control group for microbiome examinations

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
severe postnatal adjustment disorder of a newborn (asphyxia) with HIE and hypothermia treatment
Exclusion criteria:
- Preterms <35+0 gestational weeks
- Severe congenital malformations
